abstract: Loss of antigen presentation allows tumours to escape T cells and resist immune checkpoint blockade. In melanoma cell lines, several microRNAs repress genes of the antigen-presentation machinery, and many microRNAs have been proposed as immune biomarkers in melanoma tissue. Most tissue evidence comes from bulk biopsies, in which both microRNA profiles and immune-gene expression depend on the immune-cell content of the sample. Following a pre-specified analysis plan, we regressed five immune-module scores on 662 mature microRNAs in 431 melanomas from The Cancer Genome Atlas (3,310 tests), with and without adjustment for tumour purity, leukocyte content, interferon tone and clinical covariates. We labelled each microRNA by its likely cell of origin, required target-level evidence for candidates, re-tested nine published microRNA sets, and examined the antigen-presentation programme in four skin-cancer single-cell datasets, three checkpoint-blockade cohorts (155 patients) and survival data. Of 1,334 associations significant before adjustment, 82.5% were lost after it, and 188 emerged only after it. Only 20 of the 127 microRNAs associated with antigen presentation after adjustment were labelled tumour-intrinsic, and none met the target-level criterion. The closest candidate, miR-361-5p (myeloid-suppression module), failed only a multiple-testing correction added after the target-level results were known. Published sets were enriched among unadjusted antigen-presentation associations (odds ratio 3.32) but not among adjusted ones (1.02), and lost significance as often as other microRNAs (83.3% versus 85.8%). In single-cell data, non-malignant cells expressed the antigen-presentation programme more strongly than malignant cells in 19 of 20 contrasts. A higher antigen-presentation score predicted longer survival after adjustment for composition (hazard ratio 0.69) but not for interferon tone (0.86), and the immunotherapy cohorts were uninformative. In melanoma tissue, most microRNA-immune associations reflect the immune-cell content of the biopsy. Showing that microRNAs control antigen presentation in tumour cells will require compartment-resolved measurements and adequately powered target-level tests.
